newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea promises more corn aid for hungry North.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea promises more corn aid for hungry North.

text.p: South Korea on Friday pledged additional food aid worth $10 million to a U.N. appeal for North Korea, and its Red Cross proposed another round of talks with its northern counterpart on speeding relief deliveries.

The promise of 50,000 tonnes of corn and 300 tonnes of powdered milk is in addition to $6 million already delivered to the World Food Programme (WFP), which has appealed for 200,000 tonnes of aid worth $98.5 million.
The United States has pledged $25 million to the WFP to help stave off famine in the Stalinist nation.
Pyongyang has requested massive food assistance as a condition for joining proposed peace talks with South Korea, the United States and China.

But a South Korean cabinet minister on Friday again insisted that large-scale food aid could only be discussed during the four-way peace talks, and blamed Pyongyang's food crisis partly on its huge military spending.

Unification Minister Kwon O-kie told an international conference in Tokyo that Pyongyang could get more food aid and direct investment from the South by agreeing to talks aimed at establishing a permanent peace to replace the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
"By starting the four-way talks, we can implement a variety of economic measures, and this includes proposed direct investment," Kwon said.
He said North Korea spent $6 billion each year on its military and $900 million on political propaganda.
"If a fraction of this were used for the North's basic needs, the food situation would improve and the burden on their budget would be reduced significantly," Kwon said.
His comments were echoed by Unificiation Ministry spokesman Kang Ho-yang in Seoul.

"Any further aid will depend on the North's attitude. The North appears to be spending fairly lavishly for a military parade while their citizens are starving," he said, referring to ceremonies last month to mark the 65th anniversary of the founding of the Peoples' Army.
Separately, the South Korean Red Cross proposed a meeting with the North Korean Red Cross on May 23, either in Seoul, Pyongyang or at the border village of Panmunjom.
It wants to negotiate direct food shipments across the border at Panmunjom, bypassing the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies that now acts as a go-between.

But talks in Beijing on May 3 and 5 -- the first inter-Korean Red Cross meeting in nearly five years -- broke down over Pyongyang's insistence that the South first commit to a specific quantity of aid.

Kang Young-hoon, president of the Southern Red Cross, on Friday sent a message to his counterpart via a telephone hotline at Panmunjom giving an assurance that the South would give details of the size of proposed aid.
Seoul officials have said they hoped Red Cross contacts would develop into wider cross-border exchanges.

The Southern Red Cross is due to deliver 3,600 tonnes of corn by train next week from China, the first batch of 15,000 tonnes donated by civic groups, which have pledged to collect money for 95,000 tonnes of corn.
The Red Cross is the only legal channel for private aid from South Korea to the North.
